senses.definition: (theology) The chief devil; Satan.
(theology) An evil creature, the objectification of a hostile and destructive force.

(folklore) A man with red or orange skin and a pair of horns on his head, a pointed goatee, and a long tail, who carries a pitchfork, represents evil, and is portrayed to children as a boogeyman who punishes bad behavior.
The bad part of the conscience; the opposite to the angel.
examples: The devil in me wants to let him suffer.

senses.definition: A wicked or naughty person, or one who harbors reckless, spirited energy, especially in a mischievous way; usually said of a young child.
examples: Those two kids are devils in a toy store.

senses.definition: A thing that is awkward or difficult to understand or do.
examples: That math problem was a devil.

senses.definition: (euphemistic, with an article, as an intensifier) Hell.
examples: What in the devil is that?
She is having a devil of a time fixing it.
You can go to the devil for all I care.

senses.definition: A person, especially a man; used to express a particular opinion of him, usually in the phrases poor devil and lucky devil.

quotes.text: 'Well, I'm damned,' said Bond. 'Of course that old devil M never told me. He just gives one the facts. Never tells one any good news. I suppose he thinks it might influence one's decision to take a case or not.'
quotes.reference: 1954, Ian Fleming, “The Red Carpet”, in Live and Let Die, London: Pan Books, published 1957, page 8:

senses.definition: A printer's assistant.

quotes.text: For he will not leave his listener to dwell upon sorrow when the print office beckons and he can show you what a good little devil he became.
quotes.reference: 2010, Andrea Levy, The Long Song, Tinder Press (2017), page 381:

senses.definition: (India) A poltergeist that haunts printing works.
A dust devil.

quotes.text: The formation of tornados and water-spouts is very probably identical with that of dust-storms and "devils," viz., a sudden disturbance of the vertical equilibrium of the atmosphere, where by an upward rush of air is generated, which rapidly becomes spiral.
quotes.reference: 1877, H. F. Blandford, Indian Meteorologist's Vade-mecum, page 140:

quotes.text: There are few sights more appalling than a sandstorm in the desert, the "Zauba'ah" as the Arabs call it. Devils, or pillars of sand, vertical and inclined, measuring a thousand feet high[.]
quotes.reference: 1885, Richard F. Burton, chapter XII, in The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, volume I, The Burton Club, page 114 footnote:

senses.definition: (dialectal, in compounds) A barren, unproductive and unused area.
(cooking) A dish, as a bone with the meat, broiled and excessively peppered; a grill with Cayenne pepper.

quotes.text: Men and women busy in baking, broiling, roasting oysters, and preparing devils on the gridiron.
quotes.reference: 1815 February 24, [Walter Scott], Guy Mannering; or, The Astrologer. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), Edinburgh: […] James Ballantyne and Co. for Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, […]; and Archibald Constable and Co., […], →OCLC:

senses.definition: A machine for tearing or cutting rags, cotton, etc., as used in the production of mungo or shoddy.

quotes.text: The woollen things are torn to pieces by a machine having spiked rollers (termed a devil), cleansed, and the fibre spun with a certain proportion of new wool, the yarn being afterwards woven into the full-bodied but flimsy fabric termed shoddy.
quotes.reference: 1918, Henry J. Spooner, Wealth from Waste: Elimination of Waste A World Problem, George Routledge & Sons, →ISBN, →OCLC, →OL, page 200:

senses.definition: A Tasmanian devil.
examples: He removes his food, water, and torch from the pack and then pushes it to the far end of the tent – no devil is going to rip his pack apart tonight.

quotes.text: In the 1800s, for example, workers at a wool company were scared that the devils would attack their sheep.
quotes.reference: 2008, Joyce L. Markovics, Tasmanian Devil: Nighttime Scavenger, page 8:

senses.definition: (cycling, slang) An endurance event where riders who fall behind are periodically eliminated.
(nautical) Ellipsis of devil seam (“the seam between garboard strake and the keel, on wooden boats”).
To make like a devil; to invest with the character of a devil.
To annoy or bother.
(intransitive) To work as a ‘devil’; to work for a lawyer or writer without fee or recognition.

quotes.text: He did not repeat the scathing estimate of her character by Quatrefages, who at that time spent one afternoon a week devilling at the Consulate, keeping the petty-cash box in order.
quotes.reference: 1978, Lawrence Durrell, Livia (Avignon Quintet), Faber & Faber, published 1992, page 401:

senses.definition: To ghostwrite; to author while working as a ‘devil’.

quotes.text: Didn't secretaries write the speeches of Parliamentary "big-bugs"? Weren't the opinions of eminent lawyers often written by their juniors, read over and signed? Weren't briefs and pleadings devilled?

senses.definition: To prepare (food) with spices, making it spicy:

quotes.text: […]; you could watch a buckwheat pancake whirled into existence under your eyes and see fowls' legs devilled, peppered, grilled, and tormented till they lost all semblance of the original Mariposa chicken.
quotes.reference: 1912, Stephen Leacock, “The Hostelry of Mr. Smith”, in Sunshine Sketches of a Little Town, page 28:

subsenses.definition: To finely grind (cooked ham or other meat) with spices and condiments.
To prepare (shelled halved boiled eggs, as a sidedish) by removing the yolks, adding condiments and spices to them, and placing that mixture back into (the halved eggs' whites) to be served.
examples: She's going to devil four dozen eggs for the picnic.

senses.definition: To shred fabric into its fibres for recycling, as in the production of mungo or shoddy.

quotes.text: Tailors' clippings and remnants of fine woollen goods, such as broadcloth, etc., are devilled and spun into yarn for making cloth of nicer quality, called mungo.
quotes.reference: 1918, Henry J. Spooner, Wealth from Waste: Elimination of Waste A World Problem, George Routledge & Sons, →ISBN, →OCLC, →OL, page 200:
